list.listitem: Hypertensive nephropathy, or nephrosclerosis, is defined as glomerulo-vascular damage due to chronic hypertension.C

Suspect hypertensive nephropathy in patients with incidental findings of microscopic hematuria, proteinuria during routine urinalysis, signs of end-organ damage, or progressively worsening renal function. C
Definitive diagnosis is by renal biopsy, but this is not routinely recommended.C
Treatment focuses on optimal blood pressure control with an ACE or ARB and a target of 130/80 for patients with chronic kidney disease.B
Approximately one in four patients with hypertensive nephropathy will progress to end-stage renal disease (ESRD).B

background.definition: Hypertensive nephropathy can be defined as renal damage in the glomerular and vascular bed due to chronic hypertension. It can occur with or without moderate proteinuria. The pathologic picture is characterized by arteriosclerosis, arteriolosclerosis, glomerulosclerosis, and interstitial fibrosis in the absence of immune deposits.

list.listitem: The United States Renal Data System 2016 report showed that the adjusted incidence rate of ESRD from hypertension was about 100 patients per million per year.

Prevalence is difficult to estimate because the cause of chronic kidney disease may be multifactorial or difficult to ascertain. This may lead to an overestimation of prevalence, especially among African Americans.

Hypertensive nephrosclerosis accounts for 32% of kidney disease. Approximately one-quarter of patients with hypertensive nephrosclerosis eventually develop ESRD. The rate of ESRD attributed to hypertension has grown by 9% since 2000.
Hypertensive nephropathy is second only to diabetes as a leading etiology of progressive renal decline and end-stage renal disease.
Hypertensive nephrosclerosis is the second most common cause of ESRD in Caucasians (23%) and is the leading cause of ESRD in African Americans (46%).
African Americans have a sixfold risk of developing hypertensive nephropathy compared with non-Hispanic whites.
Chronically untreated high blood pressure (mean arterial blood pressure >107 mm Hg) is an independent predictor of the progression of age-related decline in renal function.
The kidney is involved in the genesis of hypertension, and the development of hypertension is believed to be the consequence of resetting the pressure-natriuresis relationship.

The vascular/endothelial response to chronic hypertension is medial hypertrophy and intimal thickening, which leads to luminal narrowing. The accompanying hypertension-related endothelial injury is hyalinosis of the vascular wall, resulting in loss of compliance of the vascular wall. This results in loss of the autoregulatory mechanisms to blood pressure variations.
Global glomerular damage due to ischemic injury results in global sclerosis and nephron loss.
There is compensatory glomerular enlargement and proteinuria, and segmental glomerular lesions develop because of loss of functioning glomeruli.
The APOL-1 gene is associated with non-diabetic chronic kidney disease and is disproportionately expressed in African Americans.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Underlying chronic renal disease of any etiology

list.listitem: Screen adults for elevated blood pressure.A
A low-salt diet, smoking cessation, and weight loss for overweight and obese patients are recommended.B
Monitor patients with hypertension for evidence of end-organ damage and progression to ESRD.B

Adults aged older than 40 years should be screened at least annually for hypertension. Adults aged 18 to 39 years should be screened annually if they have additional risk factors for hypertension or if previously measured blood pressure is between 130/85-89 mm Hg and 139/85-89 mm Hg. Otherwise, they should be screened at least every 3 years.
Use ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) or home blood pressure measurement to confirm the diagnosis of hypertension and monitor response to therapy.
The USPSTF found insufficient evidence regarding screening for chronic kidney disease, although that recommendation statement is now labeled as "inactive".
Primary prevention can be achieved by preventing the development of high blood pressure.
The DASH diet, low dietary sodium intake, and increased physical activity have been recommended to reduce the risk of developing high blood pressure based on expert opinion.
Advise and assist smokers with smoking cessation.
Maintenance of a normal BMI and weight loss have also been recommended based on expert opinion and other potential health benefits.
Regularly assess patients with hypertension for end-organ damage such as renal disease.

Treatment to a BP goal of less than 130/80 mm Hg reduces the progression of hypertensive nephropathy. However, lower blood pressure targets also increase the likelihood of adverse events, including acute renal failure, and increase the average number of medications needed.
Use an antiproteinuric antihypertensive such as an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) in patients with established proteinuria.
Guidelines recommend the albumin-to-creatinine ratio or 24-hour quantified albuminuria when evaluating patients suspected of having hypertensive renal disease.C

In patients with renal disease and chronic hypertension, obtain a renal ultrasound to assess for bilateral renal atrophy and to assess intra-parenchymal resistive indices and corticomedullary differentiation.C
Definitive diagnosis is established by renal biopsy and histology, but is recommended only for patients with other competing etiologies for chronic kidney disease.C

Differential.Differential_Features: Long-standing (especially poorly or uncontrolled) diabetes mellitus, albuminuria, progressive chronic kidney disease
Nephrotic-range proteinuria, sclerosis in parts of some of the glomeruli
Signs of glomerulonephritis occurring a few weeks post viral syndrome or bacterial infection, commonly Streptococcus sp
Involves the basement membranes of the kidney and frequently affects the cochlea and the eyes

list.listitem: Patients are asymptomatic for most of the natural history of hypertensive nephropathy. There are no specific signs or symptoms that correlate with the diagnosis of hypertensive nephropathy.
Signs of kidney disease include hematuria, foamy urine, periorbital edema, and lower extremity swelling.

The physical examination should focus on identifying end-organ damage due to long-standing hypertension, such as displaced apical impulse, S4, and retinopathy. These findings are markers of end-organ damage, which includes renal damage.

Hypertensive nephropathy can be diagnosed when hypertension is preceded by evidence of hypertensive renal injury (proteinuria and abnormal serum creatinine) after excluding other possible etiologies of renal injury.

Obtain qualitative urinalysis as part of the initial evaluation, and consider repeating it annually in hypertensive patients. Evidence of microscopic hematuria, proteinuria during routine urinalysis, or progressively worsening renal function should raise the suspicion of hypertensive nephropathy.

Blood urea nitrogen, serum creatinine, and calculation of the glomerular filtration rate are recommended as part of the initial and annual evaluation of hypertensive patients. Chronic kidney disease can be diagnosed if the decline in renal function persists beyond 3 months.

Quantifying proteinuria using albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) and 24-hour urine albumin is recommended for assessing the degree of glomerular damage.
Normal: ACR <30 mg/g or 24-hour urine albumin <30 mg/day Moderately increased (microalbuminuria): ACR 30 to 300 mg/g or 24-hour urine albumin 30 to 300 mg/day Severely increased (macroalbuminuria): ACR >300 mg/g or 24-hour urine albumin >300 mg/day

In patients with hypertension and elevated serum creatinine, obtain renal ultrasound to evaluate for bilateral renal atrophy, assess the resistive renal indices, and rule out any other etiologies of chronic renal failure.
Staging chronic renal disease related to hypertensive nephropathy requires knowledge of the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and the urine albumin level (see ).

Ultimately, the definitive diagnosis of hypertensive nephropathy can only be confirmed by biopsy. However, biopsy is recommended only for patients who have other competing etiologies for renal failure such as diabetic nephropathy, glomerulonephritis, nephrotic syndrome, and patients with autoimmune diseases like systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
See the algorithm in for a suggested approach to patients suspected of having hypertensive nephropathy.

ACC/AHA guidelines recommend a blood pressure target of 130/80 for patients with chronic kidney disease; KDIGO guidelines recommend the same target for anyone with urine albumin excretion of ≥30 mg/24 hours.A
Medication classes for controlling blood pressure should include an ACE inhibitor (ACEI) or angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) in all patients with albuminuria >300 mg/g or mg/day.A
Dietary modifications such as reduced salt and the DASH diet, exercising for 150 minutes per week, and avoiding smoking may be beneficial for lowering blood pressure.B
Treat metabolic acidosis with bicarbonate level <20 mEq sodium bicarbonate.B
Quitting smoking is associated with a slower rate of progression of GFR decline.C
Modulating or treating other risk factors, for example diabetes mellitus, can influence the progression of GFR decline.B
Appropriate blood pressure control is associated with a lower likelihood of death due to chronic kidney disease.
No association has been found between blood pressure response and the rate of renal function decline.
According to the 2017 ACC/AHA guidelines on management of blood pressure, the blood pressure goal in CKD patients should be <130/80 mm Hg.
In patients with hypertensive nephropathy with albuminuria >300 mg/day or mg/g, an ACEI or an ARB is recommended.

KDIGO guidelines regarding blood pressure targets in non-diabetic chronic kidney disease are as follows: In patients with urine albumin <30 mg/24 hours (or equivalent) whose office BP is consistently >140/90 mm Hg, maintain a BP that is consistently ≤140/90 mm Hg. In patients with urine albumin excretion of ≥30 mg/24 hours (or equivalent) whose office BP is consistently >130/80 mm Hg, maintain a BP that is consistently ≤130/80 mm Hg.

First-line treatment for blood pressure in patients with hypertensive nephrosclerosis is an ACEI or an ARB. No head-to-head trials have been done comparing ACEI and ARB or the various types of ACEI and ARBs. It is believed to be a class effect.
ACEIs and ARBs as a group decrease renal protein excretion by approximately 30% in non-diabetic CKD patients.

If ACEIs or ARBs are contraindicated, second-line agents are non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as verapamil and diltiazem. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as diltiazem and verapamil, also have significant antiproteinuric effects.
Other antihypertensive drugs have variable antiproteinuric effects and should be used in combination with ACEI/ARBs, unless there is a contraindication to ACEI/ARBs.

An RCT found that in patients with CKD and GFR between 25 and 75, with or without T2DM, dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily reduces the likelihood of death (NNT = 48) and the need for dialysis or renal transplant (NNT = 71) when taken for a median of 2.4 years.

In patients with stage IV or V chronic kidney disease, a randomized trial with 411 patients found that there was no evidence of harm and a possible reduction in the need for renal replacement therapy with continued use of an ACEI or ARB.

A systematic review found 20 RCTs with 1441 patients with hypertensive nephropathy randomizing them to alprostadil or placebo. Measures of renal function were improved but clinical outcomes were not reported.
A modest reduction in salt intake for at least 4 weeks results in a reduction in blood pressure in both hypertensive and normotensive patients.
Lifestyle modifications should include 150 minutes of aerobic exercise per week to assist with blood pressure control and prevent other cardiovascular diseases.
KDIGO guidelines recommend 30 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise on most days of the week.
On average, the rate of decline of GFR is 1 to 2 mL/min/year in patients with hypertensive nephrosclerosis, in comparison to patients with diabetic nephropathy and polycystic kidney disease.C
In proteinuric patients with hypertensive nephrosclerosis, the rate of decline of GFR is higher, at 6 to 8 mL/min/year.C
Hypertensive nephropathy is the second leading cause of ESRD.C
